g: History; Indigenous history of North America
sum: Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz retells the history of the United States from the perspective of Indigenous peoples, arguing that the nation was founded on settler colonialism: a deliberate policy of taking land and eliminating or removing its inhabitants. From pre-contact societies through colonisation, removal, the reservation era and modern activism, she challenges the myths of discovery and frontier.
bg: Published in 2014 as part of Beacon Press’s ReVisioning American History series, the book won an American Book Award. Dunbar-Ortiz is a historian, activist and long-time participant in the American Indian Movement and international Indigenous rights work. A young readers’ adaptation appeared in 2019.
br: The opening chapters on Indigenous societies before European arrival set up the argument; later chapters move quickly through centuries, so a timeline or map can help keep events in order.
la: Dunbar-Ortiz writes argumentative history, naming policies and their architects directly and connecting past violence to present law, land and military doctrine. Her tone is uncompromising and her framing explicit from the first page.
cx: The book belongs to a wider scholarly movement to centre Indigenous perspectives and the concept of settler colonialism; some readers and historians dispute aspects of its framing and emphasis.
th: Settler colonialism
Taking land and removing peoples was a deliberate, continuous policy.
Resistance and survival
Indigenous nations resisted and persist with living cultures.
Myth and memory
National myths of discovery and frontier hide violence.
fit: Pairs with Killers of the Flower Moon and A People’s History of the United States on your list.
mis: Its uncompromising argument and condensed coverage of centuries may feel polemical or rushed to some readers.
rq: What does settler colonialism mean in practice?
How does the book connect past to present?
dq: How should national history handle genocide?
What would justice for Indigenous nations look like today?

g: Russian novel; realist family and social novel
sum: Anna Karenina, married to a cold senior official in St Petersburg, falls passionately in love with the dashing officer Vronsky and defies society to be with him, at enormous cost. In counterpoint, the awkward, idealistic landowner Levin pursues Kitty, struggles with farming and faith, and searches for a meaningful life. Around them Tolstoy paints the whole of Russian society.
bg: Tolstoy published the novel in instalments from 1875 to 1877, with the complete book appearing in 1878. It followed War and Peace and is often called one of the greatest novels ever written. Its famous opening line declares that all happy families are alike, while each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
br: Long, but structured in eight parts with short chapters. Keep a character list handy for the Russian names and patronymics. Modern translations by Pevear and Volokhonsky, Rosamund Bartlett or Marian Schwartz are all well regarded.
la: Tolstoy moves effortlessly between minds, giving even minor characters and a dog their own inner lives. The parallel stories of Anna and Levin mirror and comment on each other without ever being forced together.
cx: The novel reflects debates in 1870s Russia about marriage, divorce, women’s position, agricultural reform and religion, and Tolstoy’s own growing spiritual crisis, which shaped Levin’s story.
th: Love and society
Passion collides with rigid social rules, and women pay most.
Searching for meaning
Levin seeks faith and purpose in work, family and nature.
Family happiness
Ordinary domestic life can be the hardest and most meaningful achievement.
fit: A cornerstone of the Russian classics on your list, alongside War and Peace and the Dostoevsky novels.
mis: Long, with extended passages on farming and politics that some readers find slow.
rq: How does Tolstoy make Anna sympathetic?
Why does the novel give Levin so much space?
How do the two stories comment on each other?
dq: Is Anna a victim, a heroine, or both?
rel: War and Peace, Tolstoy’s earlier epic.
Tolstoy’s later, darker view of marriage.

g: Russian novella; moral and social argument
sum: On a long train journey, a passenger named Pozdnyshev tells a stranger how jealousy, sexual obsession and a bitter marriage led him to murder his wife, after she played Beethoven’s Kreutzer Sonata with a violinist. His confession becomes a fierce attack on marriage, sexual desire and the way society raises men and women.
bg: Written in 1889, after Tolstoy’s religious conversion, the novella was censored in Russia, banned in the United States from the mail, and caused a scandal across Europe. Tolstoy added an afterword defending its views on chastity. Janáček later wrote a string quartet inspired by it.
br: Short enough to read in a sitting or two. Remember that Pozdnyshev is a narrator in crisis; ask how far Tolstoy shares his views and how far the story exposes them.
la: The frame of a confession on a train creates claustrophobic intensity, and Tolstoy uses music, especially the Beethoven sonata, as a force that disturbs the characters’ self-control. Pozdnyshev’s voice is feverish and repetitive, which is part of the effect.
cx: The work reflects Tolstoy’s late moral philosophy of chastity and nonviolence, and the strained marriage of Tolstoy and his wife Sophia, who wrote her own reply to it.
th: Jealousy and possession
Obsessive jealousy turns love into ownership and finally violence.
Sexual morality
Tolstoy attacks desire and marriage as sources of misery.
Music and emotion
Art can overwhelm reason and stir feelings people cannot control.
fit: A short, intense counterpoint to Anna Karenina and The Death of Ivan Ilyich on your list.
mis: Its views on sex, women and marriage are extreme and many readers find them repellent.
rq: How reliable is Pozdnyshev as a narrator?
What role does the music play?
How far does Tolstoy share his narrator’s views?
dq: Is the novella an argument or a portrait of madness?
How does it compare with Anna Karenina?

g: Russian autobiographical fiction; trilogy of novellas
sum: Tolstoy’s first published work follows Nikolenka Irtenev from the age of ten through boyhood into early adulthood: a beloved mother and tutor, the move to Moscow, the first experiences of death and shame, intense friendships, university and the agonies of wanting to be thought comme il faut. It is a portrait of a growing mind, full of fine observation and self-scrutiny.
bg: Childhood appeared in 1852 in the journal The Contemporary, followed by Boyhood in 1854 and Youth in 1857. Though drawn from Tolstoy’s own life and family, it is fiction, and it launched his literary career while he was serving as a young army officer in the Caucasus.
br: Read the three parts in order as one book. The episodes are short and self-contained, and the pleasure lies in the precise remembered details rather than plot. It is a good warm-up before the longer novels.
la: Tolstoy pioneers the close psychological observation that would mark his great novels, alternating between the child’s experience and the older narrator’s reflective, often ironic commentary. Chapters such as Maman and Grief show this double vision at its finest.
cx: The trilogy reflects Russian gentry life in the 1830s and 1840s and shows Tolstoy already preoccupied with sincerity, vanity, death and moral self-improvement. Turgenev and Nekrasov recognised the young author’s gifts immediately.
th: Memory
The past is recreated through vivid, precise remembered details.
Self-consciousness
Growing up means learning to watch, doubt and judge oneself.
Moral striving
Nikolenka’s wish to be good wars constantly with vanity and pride.
fit: A gentle introduction to Tolstoy’s mind, linking War and Peace, Anna Karenina and The Death of Ivan Ilyich on your list.
mis: Episodic and plotless; readers who want drama may find it slight. The final part can feel unfinished.
rq: Which childhood memory felt most true to you?
How does the narrator judge his younger self?
How does Nikolenka change across the three parts?
dq: What seeds of the later Tolstoy do you see here?

sum: The Devil, calling himself Professor Woland, arrives in 1930s Moscow with a retinue that includes a giant talking cat, and sets about exposing the greed, cowardice and hypocrisy of Soviet literary and bureaucratic life. Interwoven are the story of the Master, a persecuted writer of a novel about Pontius Pilate, and Margarita, who makes a pact with Woland to save him.
bg: Mikhail Bulgakov wrote the novel in secret from 1928 until his death in 1940. It was published in censored form in 1966–67 and uncensored only later, and it became a cult classic in the Soviet Union and beyond.
br: Expect three interwoven strands: satirical Moscow chaos, the Pilate chapters set in ancient Jerusalem, and the love story. They connect in surprising ways, so be patient with the early chapters.
la: Bulgakov combines slapstick comedy, biting satire, gothic fantasy and lyrical romance, and the Jerusalem chapters are written in a starkly different, solemn style. The tonal range is part of the novel’s argument about freedom and imagination.
cx: The novel satirises Stalinist censorship, informers and literary bureaucracy, and Bulgakov’s own work was banned during his lifetime, which gives the Master’s story painful resonance. Bulgakov even wrote a personal letter to Stalin asking to emigrate.
th: Art and censorship
Manuscripts don’t burn: true art can outlive repression and censorship.
Good and evil
The Devil exposes human hypocrisy more than he causes any evil.
Love and courage
Margarita’s devotion is the novel’s great act of love and courage.
fit: A wildly inventive Russian classic that balances the realists on your list with fantasy and satire.
mis: Its structure and satire of Soviet life can confuse readers without some context.
rq: What is Woland’s role in Moscow?
How do the Pilate chapters connect to the rest?
dq: What does the novel say about art under tyranny?
